posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md: Saxby suggests using a black magic marker to paint the edges of plates to prevent light from entering. For something even better than a black magic marker, go to Michael's (craft store) and buy a 'DecoColor (tm) Opaque Paint Marker' (color: black). These have real paint in them - much more opaque than magic markers.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
> **dave battin:** Tony ,do you have to remove it befor it goes into the developer ?

Almost certainly yes - use Kleenex dampened with isopropanol to wipe it off, otherwise little black flakes will float off in the developer and deposit on your plate. I have not yet found a marker that resists alkaline developer - even Kodak negative grease pencils wash off!

Another good black marker available at art stores is Sakura's "Permapaque" opaque pigment marker. It's water based, but somewhat water resistant when dry. Very black on glass!

The best of the non-pigment markers (my previous favorite) is Staedtler's Lumocolor 357 permanent. Not quite so black, but it coats glass a little better and is less likely to rub off with handling.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: I take a piece of black electrical tape and tape it down on a piece of glass. I then take a plate the same size I am shooting and put the edge of it on the tape. I then cut the tape with a razor blade such that it is the same size at the edge of the plate. Then peel it off and put it on the plate to be shot. I found I can use the same piece of tape a few times before the stickyness wears out.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: I have used tape and markers but making a film holder to block the light is best.

Agreed, except when you want to minimize the thickness of the plate edge shadow in single-beam Denisyuks.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: Yes, this takes some design. I beveled my film holder to 45 deg rees to the plate but it still leaves a small shadow. One would use 56 but it would take a different set up than I had at the time. I made the relief with a router in aluminum. If I had used a table saw or a mill I could have gotten it to brewsters angle.
